edition: Issue 047: New Zealand is officially the world's cheat code for GTA 6, India's pace factory brings a good headache to the Basin, and a half-price robot accountant moves next door to Xero
tagline: Your 3-minute Wednesday reset: the year's biggest video game unlocks here first, four Indian quicks test the Wellington wind, and the AI bookkeeper taking aim at Xero.

stories.headline: GTA 6 unlocks at midnight — and New Zealand is the first place in the world playing it
stories.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI unlocks worldwide at midnight local time on 19 November, so New Zealand players get in first; Rockstar's twice-delayed mega-sequel follows crime-and-romance duo Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos — the series' first female playable lead since GTA III in 2001 — across a Florida-inspired Leonida roughly double the size of GTA V's map.

body.text: Grand Theft Auto VI — the most anticipated video game of a generation and the biggest entertainment launch in years — releases worldwide at midnight local time on 19 November, which means New Zealand players are among the first on Earth to play it. Rockstar Games delayed the sequel twice (first promised for 2025, moved to 26 May 2026, then to 19 November 2026), saying it needed the extra months to hit the standard it wanted, and rival studios shifted their own release dates to avoid the clash. The game follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos — partners in crime and love — through Leonida, a fictional, Florida-inspired state, with Lucia the first female playable character since the series introduced fully fledged protagonists in GTA III back in 2001. The map is roughly twice the size of GTA V's (about 50 to 75 square kilometres) and takes in Vice City, the setting of the beloved 1980s-themed 2002 game. The stakes: GTA V sold more than 230 million copies in its 13 years on sale. The cost of entry this time: a download of more than 200GB — about 212GB on PS5 and 234GB on Xbox Series X|S — with pre-loading available since last week.

Deep breaths, workers of New Zealand: that mystery cough sweeping the office this week is completely real and absolutely not a 212-gigabyte man-flu cover story. And let's give our timezone its flowers. After decades of being the country that watches World Cup finals at 5am, we are now officially the cheat code of Planet Earth — the game unlocks from our midnight outwards, Melbourne plays three hours before Perth (correct behaviour, frankly), and the only humans ahead of us live in Kiribati, who have won at timezones so thoroughly they say first all year round. Rockstar deserves a serve too: full price for a cardboard box containing one piece of paper with a code on it — digital convenience or packaging fraud, you decide — and the hacking group that leaked the near-finished game dressed itself up as consumer-rights activism before it turned out to be a crypto scam, somehow the least absurd part of the whole saga. Nicest plot twist of all: the first female playable lead in a quarter of a century. Slowest character unlock in entertainment history — but she is finally here, and honestly, partners-in-crime-and-love is already a better love story than this franchise has managed since Vice City.

RNZ (18 Nov 2026, Gianfranco Di Giovanni and Kyle Pauletto, Grand Theft Auto 6 is out this week — here is everything you need to know): GTA 6 is available at midnight local time on 19 November 2026 per a Rockstar Games support post, making New Zealand players among the first in the world; the game is set in Leonida, a fictional Florida-inspired state, following Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, partners in crime and love; Lucia is the first female playable character since the series introduced fully fledged protagonists in GTA III (2001); the playable area is roughly twice the size of GTA V, about 50 to 75 square kilometres, and includes Vice City, setting of the 1980s-themed 2002 game; GTA V sold more than 230 million copies in 13 years; the game was promised for 2025, moved to 26 May 2026, then to 19 November 2026, with other developers moving their release dates to avoid the clash; the download is more than 200GB — about 212GB on PS5 and 234GB on Xbox Series X|S — with pre-loading since last week; in June 2026 Rockstar said boxed copies would contain only a digital download code, not a disc, sparking a backlash; hacking group CyberLeek released footage of the near-finished product and threatened more leaks unless Rockstar changed its disc policy, with crypto-scam motives later revealed; GTA 5 was pulled from Kmart and Target shelves in Australia in 2014 after a Change.org petition topped 47,000 signatures.

stories.headline: India's 'good headache': a four-pronged pace attack, the Wellington wind, and a series with the Black Caps starting Thursday
stories.summary: India plan to field four frontline quicks — with Jasprit Bumrah back leading the attack — for the first Test against the Black Caps at the Basin Reserve from Thursday, after sweeping the preceding T20 and ODI series; captain Shubman Gill calls the selection logjam a good headache, and Rishabh Pant returns from a side strain chasing his first Test hundred in New Zealand.

body.text: India will field four frontline fast bowlers in the first Test against New Zealand, which starts at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday — a selection problem captain Shubman Gill calls a bit of a headache, but the good kind of headache to have. Jasprit Bumrah returns to lead the pace attack, and Mohammed Siraj is likely to keep his place after the tourists won the preceding Twenty20 and one-day international series. Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj could edge out Prasidh Krishna and Gurnoor Brar in part because they can contribute with the bat lower down the order. Gill wants four fast-bowling options covering all the aspects, noting Basin pitches can go flat with the old ball on days three to five and that the wind will make one end harder to bowl into. Rishabh Pant returns from a side strain to take the gloves; as Gill noted, Pant has scored Test hundreds in Australia, South Africa and England — New Zealand is the only country where he hasn't.

India's good headache is the most expensive medical condition in sport: too many world-class fast bowlers and only eleven spots on the team sheet. Over here we call that a selection crisis; over there they call it Tuesday. Bumrah leading the attack again is the cricketing equivalent of your landlord ringing to say he's redecorating the kitchen — technically fine, but you know something is coming. And the Basin Reserve wind returns to play the 12th man yet again: the only cricketer in the world who shows up without a contract and still moves the ball around. As for Pant — hundreds in Australia, South Africa and England, and the one country left on the list is the one with two islands, one permanent weather front and a coffee culture that refuses to start before 10.30am. We would say he is not beating the allegations, but honestly, we are just excited to see him try.

RNZ / Reuters (18 Nov 2026, 6:07am, Gill faces good headache as India line up pace quartet to take on Black Caps in Wellington): India will field four frontline pacers in the opening Test of a two-match series beginning at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday; Jasprit Bumrah returns to lead the pace attack and Mohammed Siraj is likely to keep his place after India won the preceding Twenty20 and one-day international series; Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj are in contention partly because they can contribute with the bat lower down the order, ahead of Prasidh Krishna and Gurnoor Brar; Gill said it is a bit of a headache but the good kind, wants four fast-bowling options covering all aspects, and noted wickets go flat with the old ball on days three to five; Rishabh Pant returns from a side strain; Gill noted Pant has scored Test hundreds in Australia, South Africa and England, with New Zealand the only country where he hasn't.

stories.headline: COUNT raises $11.5m to take on Xero — from Xero's own city
stories.summary: Wellington–Seattle accounting platform COUNT has raised an oversubscribed US$6.5m (NZ$11.5m) seed round led by US tax and advisory firm KBF — which runs its own books on the software — to push its AI-native, half-price bookkeeping into Xero's home market, with co-founder Chris Smith calling the Wellington base definitely a strategic choice.

body.text: If you are going to take on a giant, the least you can do is move in next door. COUNT — a Kiwi-American accounting fintech with offices in both Wellington and Seattle — has done exactly that: co-founder Chris Smith calls the Wellington base definitely a strategic choice, given rival Xero is headquartered in the same city. COUNT has raised NZ$11.5m (US$6.5m) in an oversubscribed seed round led by KBF, a 10-office US tax and advisory firm that is also a live customer — its chief executive Peter Buss calls COUNT the most AI-forward accounting solution in the market, and says KBF recommends it to clients. New Zealand funder Global From Day 1 and existing US investor Data Tech Fund also took part. The pitch: accounting software is stuck in the cloud era — Smith describes Xero's software as designed 20 years ago, while crediting Xero for driving the charge of cloud accounting — and COUNT wants to lead the next era, from cloud to AI to real-time data, at about half the cost of competing services. The platform covers records, invoicing, documents, reporting, bank reconciliation, payroll and time and billing across multiple currencies, entities and tax regimes, and opens its data to AI agents via APIs and MCP tools — just some fancy acronyms, says Smith — so a business owner can simply ask how was my company doing. The software launched last year and COUNT has about 40 staff, with support teams in Ethiopia, Norway, Australia and Canada. No valuation or revenue projections were disclosed.

An accounting startup that named itself in all caps, picked two of the windiest, wettest cities on the planet on purpose, then announced it is taking on Xero from the same street the incumbent grew up on — say what you like about COUNT's odds, the audacity is booking. Half the price, and the same familiar acronyms: API and MCP, which together translate as we will call you back. The natural-language bit is the real plot twist, though: how was my company doing used to cost you a lunch with your accountant, and now it is about to cost roughly half of that. The squeeze on the billable hour is coming for all of us, and the one job everyone quietly agreed AI should take was, obviously, this one. We admit to mixed feelings about letting software do our accounts — mostly because it will take one look at our expense claims and ask for a refund on itself.

RNZ (17 Nov 2026, 9:20am, Nona Pelletier, COUNT raises 11.5 million seed capital for its AI-based accounting software): Wellington–Seattle-based COUNT raised NZ$11.5m (US$6.5m) in an oversubscribed seed round led by US tax and advisory firm KBF, with NZ funder Global From Day 1 and other investors including existing US investor Data Tech Fund; pricing is about half the cost of competing services; co-founder Chris Smith said basing in Wellington was a strategic choice given Xero's headquarters there, described Xero's software as designed 20 years ago while crediting Xero with driving cloud accounting, and framed COUNT as leading the move from cloud to AI to real-time data; the platform covers records, invoicing, documents, reporting, bank reconciliation, payroll and time and billing, with APIs and MCP at its core; KBF chief executive Peter Buss: COUNT is the most AI-forward accounting solution in the market; COUNT launched last year with 40 staff and support teams in Ethiopia, Norway, Australia and Canada; no valuation or revenue projections disclosed. NZ Herald (16 Nov 2026, Chris Keall, premium): COUNT is a Kiwi-American fintech building AI-native accounting software across two cities with bad weather, good tech scenes in common — Seattle and Wellington; co-founder Chris Smith previously held senior roles at Amazon and Meta; COUNT charges no usage-based API fees. COUNT press release (16 Nov 2026, getcount.com): US$6.5m oversubscribed seed round led by KBF Advisory, which runs its firm on COUNT; backed by GD1, Data Tech Fund, First Row Partners, Alliance of Angels and accounting firms.
